idiom_name: sealed interface + data-class operations + exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Sealed interfaces (Kotlin 1.5+) give the compiler a known-closed algebra and `when` over it is checked for exhaustiveness when used as an expression - no `else` branch, and a new operation breaks every interpreter at compile time. Operations are data classes, so programs are immutable, structurally comparable values and interpreters are ordinary functions (or a `Fun`/`Interpreter` interface when several runtimes must be substituted). Kotlin's coroutines cover the sequencing of effects, but `suspend` functions execute when called, so they are not data: keep this pattern where the program must be inspected, tested by value or replayed, and use coroutines/Flow inside the interpreter. Where effects never need reification, plain interfaces plus constructor injection remain the simpler local idiom.
code_sketch:
sealed interface Op
data class Get(val key: String) : Op
data class Put(val key: String, val value: Int) : Op

fun run(op: Op, store: Store): Int = when (op) {
    is Get -> store.read(op.key)
    is Put -> store.write(op.key, op.value)   // no else: exhaustive
}
pitfalls: Sealed implementations may live in different files of the same package/module but not in another module, and adding an operation forces a recompilation of the module that owns the algebra.
`when` on a non-sealed interface, or on a sealed type seen only through a Java class, is not proven exhaustive - the compiler then requires `else` and the guarantee is gone.
Data classes generate structural equals/hashCode over all properties: a mutable collection property breaks value semantics of programs and test expectations.
